prohibited_recommendations: Do not start valproate: it is not first-line for focal epilepsy and, under the 2024 MHRA rules, is not started under 55 unless two specialists document that no alternative works.
Do not perform LP without indication.
Do not start an enzyme-inducing ASM (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate above 200 mg/day) while she relies on the combined oral contraceptive.
required_recommendations: Start lamotrigine or levetiracetam as first-line monotherapy for focal epilepsy, chosen for compatibility with her combined oral contraceptive (lamotrigine needs a higher dose because ethinylestradiol roughly halves its levels; levetiracetam needs mood monitoring with her anxiety disorder).
Discuss contraception and pregnancy plans before choosing the ASM; start folic acid.
Test HLA-B*15:02 before any carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.
Give kitchen and work safety advice: no cooking or working alone at hot stoves or fryers until seizures are controlled, and showers rather than baths.
Advise no driving until the locally applicable seizure-free interval is met and explain the duty to inform the licensing authority.
Counsel on SUDEP risk and how seizure control reduces it.

avoided_actions.rationale: Afebrile, no meningism or immunosuppression, and back to baseline: there is no indication for lumbar puncture.
Regular rhythm without murmur, no exertional event or cardiac history, and the semiology is epileptic: echocardiography has no indication.
Olfactory aura, automatisms and postictal confusion make syncope unlikely and the ECG is normal: ambulatory cardiac monitoring has no indication.
Back to baseline with a normal examination, no injury from the fall and no anticoagulation: emergency CT is not indicated, and the epilepsy-protocol MRI answers the structural question.
FDG-PET adds nothing to a first diagnosis with concordant MRI and EEG; it belongs to presurgical evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Chanthavong is a 19-year-old left-handed female restaurant worker who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure that occurred at home earlier today. Her partner reports that they were preparing dinner together when the patient suddenly stopped what she was doing, appeared to stare blankly ahead, and began making chewing movements with her jaw while her right hand picked repetitively at her apron. He called her name repeatedly but she did not respond. After approximately 20 seconds of this behavior, her body stiffened and she fell to the floor, followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs lasting roughly 60 to 90 seconds. She was briefly cyanotic around her lips during the convulsive phase. She bit her tongue during the event. There was no urinary incontinence. Afterward, she was confused and unable to speak coherently for approximately 20 minutes, then gradually became drowsy and fell asleep for about two hours before arriving at the emergency department.

On interview, the patient reports that just before the episode she perceived a strong, unpleasant smell that she describes as something like burning rubber, accompanied by a wave of nausea rising from her abdomen into her chest. She recalls nothing after that until waking up feeling exhausted and sore. She further reports that she has experienced similar episodes of perceiving a foul smell followed by nausea and a feeling of detachment approximately five to six times over the past eight months. These episodes would last 30 to 90 seconds and resolve spontaneously, leaving her feeling briefly disoriented. On two occasions, coworkers noticed her staring and being unresponsive for a short period, but she dismissed these as stress-related episodes. She has never previously sought medical attention for these events. She denies any recent head trauma, febrile illness, sleep deprivation beyond her normal schedule, or medication changes. She has no history of meningitis or encephalitis. She reports drinking one glass of wine the evening prior to the seizure, which is within her normal pattern.

Facial sensation symmetric to light touch in all divisions of CN V. Corneal reflexes intact bilaterally. Face symmetric with normal activation. Hearing intact bilaterally to finger rub. Palate elevates symmetrically, uvula midline. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius full strength bilaterally. Tongue midline without atrophy or fasciculations.

Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Registration 3/3, recall 3/3 at five minutes. Able to spell WORLD backwards correctly. Appears mildly anxious but cooperative.
